summary: Reproduces an ISO protocol that lets end systems and intermediate systems exchange configuration and routing information. This helps the Network Layer do its routing and relaying work, and is meant to be used alongside ISO 8473 (CLNP). It is part of the OSI set of standards.

eli5.summary: Computers and the routers near them need to introduce themselves. This protocol is how a computer says "I'm here" and a router says "I can take your mail further."

questions: how do end systems find intermediate systems in osi
subtitle: How end systems and routers discover each other in OSI networks.

tldr.problem: In OSI networks using ISO 8473 (CLNP), end systems and intermediate systems (routers) need to discover each other and exchange routing information to communicate across subnets, but there was no standard mechanism for this on-subnet discovery.
tldr.mechanism: End systems broadcast hello messages (ESH PDUs) to announce their NSAP addresses, routers broadcast hello messages (ISH PDUs) to announce their existence, and routers send redirect messages (RD PDUs) to inform end systems of better routes to destinations.
tldr.outcome: The protocol became part of the ISO 9542 standard for OSI routing and enabled end systems to dynamically discover nearby routers without manual configuration. It was eventually superseded by simpler and more scalable routing approaches in IP networks.

today: RFC 995 defined a standard mechanism for OSI networks using ISO 8473. The protocol became part of ISO 9542 (OSI Routing) but never achieved widespread deployment as IP networks (using RFC 791 and simpler routing approaches) became dominant. Modern IP networks use ARP for link-layer discovery and ICMP Router Discovery or DHCPv6 for router learning, rather than this protocol.

sections.title: Routing Discovery in OSI Networks
sections.content:
RFC 995 defines the End System to Intermediate System Routing Exchange Protocol (ES-IS), a protocol that allows end systems (hosts) and intermediate systems (routers) on the same subnetwork to discover each other and exchange routing information. Published in April 1986 as an ISO standard, it was designed for networks using ISO 8473 (the OSI Connectionless Network Protocol, or CLNP).

The protocol solves two key problems. First, how do end systems discover routers that can forward packets to distant destinations? Second, how do routers discover which end systems are on their attached subnetwork? ES-IS also allows routers to tell end systems about better routes to use for particular destinations, reducing the complexity of routing decisions in host software and improving network performance.
sections.eli5: Computers need to find routers, and routers need to find computers on the same wire. ES-IS is how they introduce themselves and where routers tell computers "Use me for that destination."

sections.title: Configuration Information and System Discovery
sections.content:
ES-IS provides two types of information: configuration information and route redirection information. Configuration information enables dynamic discovery. End systems broadcast End System Hello (ESH) PDUs containing their NSAP addresses (network addresses). Intermediate systems broadcast Intermediate System Hello (ISH) PDUs containing their Network Entity Title (an identifier for the router) and SNPA addresses (subnetwork attachment points). This is how systems on the same subnetwork learn of each other's existence without manual configuration.

On a broadcast subnetwork (like a LAN), an end system discovers all available routers and can choose among them. An intermediate system learns the addresses of all end systems on its attached subnetwork, which allows it to advertise reachability information to other routers for those destinations. On point-to-point subnetworks (like serial links), the configuration information simply verifies that both ends of the link are working. The protocol uses timers to age out old configuration information and detect when systems become unreachable.
sections.eli5: Every computer periodically says "I'm here at this address" and every router periodically says "I'm here, I can forward packets." They listen for each other's announcements to know who is available.

sections.title: Route Redirection and Better Path Learning
sections.content:
After a router receives packets from an end system, it can send a Redirect (RD) PDU to inform the end system of a better route to the destination. The redirect tells the end system "I received your packet bound for address X; send future packets for that address to router Y instead" (where Y could be another router or even the destination system itself if it is on the same subnetwork as the source). This allows the end system to cache the suggestion and optimize future traffic without requiring complex routing algorithms in the host.

Redirects are particularly valuable in networks where multiple routers are available. By learning which router is closer to a destination, end systems can balance traffic and reduce latency. The protocol includes timers to manage the lifetime of redirects, ensuring that if topology changes, stale redirect information is eventually flushed. Proper handling of redirect timers is critical to prevent persistent routing loops or inefficiencies.
sections.eli5: A router can tell a computer "I just saw your packet to address X; next time, send X's packets to that other router instead—it's closer." The computer remembers this hint.

sections.title: Protocol Data Unit Formats
sections.content:
ES-IS defines three protocol data unit (PDU) types. Each PDU begins with a fixed header containing the Network Layer Protocol Identifier (NLPID), a length indicator, a version/protocol identifier extension, a type code, a holding time, and a checksum. The holding time indicates how long the information in the PDU is valid; receiving systems discard information after this period expires.

The End System Hello (ESH) PDU contains the source system's NSAP address. The Intermediate System Hello (ISH) PDU contains the router's Network Entity Title and any number of SNPA addresses through which it can be reached. The Redirect (RD) PDU contains a destination NSAP address that triggered the redirect, a better destination address (another router or the destination itself), and optionally the SNPA address of the better route. All PDUs can carry optional parameters for security, quality of service, and priority. The protocol uses the Connectionless Network Protocol (ISO 8473) as its underlying transport.
sections.eli5: Hello messages say "I'm here." Redirect messages say "use that router instead for this address." Each message has a time limit so old information expires.

sections.title: Subnetwork Types and Applicability
sections.content:
The protocol is applicable to three types of subnetworks. On point-to-point subnetworks (two systems connected by a link), ES-IS configuration information simply establishes that both ends are reachable and determines whether both are end systems or at least one is a router. Route redirection is not used because there are no alternate paths.

On broadcast subnetworks (LANs like Ethernet), the protocol allows end systems to discover all available routers and intermediate systems to discover all end systems. This enables dynamic routing without manual configuration. On general topology subnetworks (networks that can route packets themselves but only at the subnetwork layer), the protocol provides similar functionality with less efficiency. The protocol assumes that the underlying subnetwork can deliver packets to single destinations and optionally to broadcast or multicast addresses, but it does not assume the subnetwork understands NSAP addresses.
sections.eli5: The protocol works on point-to-point links (just two things connected), broadcast networks (everyone can hear everyone), and complex networks (that have their own routing). It adapts to what the network can do.
